Re: AI‑Enabled Optimization of Early‑Phase Clinical Trials Pilot Program; Request for Information
Docket No. FDA‑2026‑N‑4390

To the Food and Drug Administration,

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the AI‑Enabled Optimization of Early‑Phase Clinical Trials Pilot Program. I am submitting this comment as an individual consumer and full‑time caregiver for my wife, who is in her fifth year of Alzheimer’s disease. I speak not only for my own family, but for millions of caregivers worldwide who urgently need progress in early‑phase clinical development.

The FDA’s notice recognizes that early‑phase trials face significant challenges: uncertainty in dose selection, limited patient populations, slow decision‑making, and the need for improved safety monitoring and biomarker‑driven evaluation. These challenges are especially acute in Alzheimer’s disease, where time is not a luxury families can afford.

I respectfully urge the FDA to ensure that this pilot program includes Alzheimer’s disease as a priority therapeutic area and encourages the evaluation of two promising neuroprotective compounds: FLAV‑27 and P7C3‑A20. Both have demonstrated strong preclinical potential in neuronal protection, inflammation reduction, and NAD⁺ pathway support — mechanisms that align directly with the pilot’s goals of improving early‑phase efficiency, safety, and decision quality through AI‑enabled tools.

Why These Compounds Fit the Pilot’s Objectives
The FDA highlights the potential for AI to enhance dose‑finding, adaptive trial design, safety monitoring, and biomarker assessment. FLAV‑27 and P7C3‑A20 are well‑suited for such an approach because:

Their biological effects can be measured through established biomarkers, including NAD⁺ restoration and neuroinflammation markers.

AI‑enabled adaptive designs could rapidly identify safe starting doses and optimize escalation strategies.

AI‑supported safety monitoring could protect elderly participants, who are often excluded from traditional early‑phase trials.

AI‑driven patient stratification could help identify responders more efficiently, reducing trial size and duration.

These capabilities directly address the early‑phase challenges outlined in the FDA’s notice.

A Compassionate and Ethical Approach
Given the progressive and irreversible nature of Alzheimer’s disease, I encourage the FDA to consider allowing early‑phase trials within this pilot to minimize or avoid placebo‑only arms for elderly participants. With AI‑enabled monitoring and adaptive designs, it is possible to uphold scientific rigor while also honoring the dignity and safety of vulnerable patients.

Families living with Alzheimer’s do not have years to wait. Every month matters.

A Global Opportunity
Alzheimer’s is a worldwide crisis. A pilot program that accelerates early‑phase evaluation of FLAV‑27 and P7C3‑A20 would:

Provide hope to millions of caregivers and patients.

Demonstrate how AI can shorten the path from discovery to human testing.

Establish a model for ethical, efficient early‑phase trials in neurodegenerative disease.

Align with the FDA’s stated goals of improving trial efficiency, safety, and decision quality.

Closing
I respectfully ask the FDA to:

Include Alzheimer’s disease as a priority therapeutic area in this pilot.

Encourage sponsors to bring FLAV‑27 and P7C3‑A20 into AI‑enabled early‑phase evaluation.

Support compassionate, biomarker‑driven, AI‑optimized trial designs that reduce unnecessary delays for elderly participants.

Thank you for considering the perspective of caregivers who live this reality every day. Your leadership in modernizing early‑phase trials has the potential to change the future for countless families.

Respectfully submitted,
Paul Sargent
Huntsville, Alabama
Individual Consumer / Caregiver Advocate
